1968 Dodge Coronet Parked for Decades Gets Second Chance, It's a Rare R/T Convertible
13 photos
Photo: Steve Magnante/YouTube
Originally introduced as a full-size car in 1949, the Dodge Coronet was discontinued after 10 years on the market. It returned in 1965, but it was repositioned as an intermediate model. The Coronet was the brand's bread-and-butter mid-size car throughout the 1960s, as well as the base for the Charger and Super Bee muscle cars.
But while it may be overshadowed by the latter, the Coronet was an integral part of the muscle car wars. When ordered in two-door body styles, it was available with the same high-performance engines as the Charger and Super Bee, including the mighty 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8.
Moreover, and this is a fact that many people miss, it was Dodge's first vehicle to sport the R/T emblem. Although the badge is more commonly associated with the Charger, the Coronet was the first to get it. Dodge introduced the Coronet R/T in 1967, a full year before the Charger.
The R/T stood for Road and Track and hinted that the said Coronet was also suitable for racing. Dodge likely had the drag strip in mind. Unlike the standard Coronet or the 500 version, the R/T came standard with the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) V8 , rated at 375 horsepower. The Hemi was optional. The Charger R/T arrived in 1968 with similar specs.
While the Coronet was a hot seller, the R/T version brought notably fewer customers into showrooms. In 1967, only 10,809 of the around 180,000 units sold were R/Ts (about 6%). In 1968, production remained similar at 10,849 examples (out of 196,000 units—5.5%). Sales dropped to 7,200 units in 1969 (4.1%) and 2,615 examples in 1970 (2.3%).
The Hemi version is obviously the rarest. Dodge sold fewer than 1,400 units between 1966 and 1970. About half of them were delivered in 1966, when the R/T wasn't available. So we're actually looking at only 637 examples with both the R/T and Hemi. But the convertible body style is also pretty rare.
Combining the retractable top and the Hemi gives us outstandingly low numbers , but the drop-top alone is scarce in R/T format. Only 1,760 rolled off the assembly line over four model years, most of them equipped with the four-barrel 440 V8. The derelict convertible you see here is one of those cars.
Found by classic car enthusiast Steve Magnante somewhere in Massachusetts, this Mopar is one of nearly 11,000 Coronet R/Ts sold in 1968. However, the convertible body style narrows that number to only 519 examples. The car was born with the three-speed automatic, and existing records say that 423 units were built in this exact drivetrain configuration.
It's quite the rare Mopar, but it's also in pretty bad shape. Based on the amount of rust covering the body, this Coronet spent a few good decades off the road. In fact, I'm pretty sure that it sat under full exposure to the elements. Some of the interior was gutted, while the original V8 engine is no longer under the hood.
The car still has a 440 V8 in the bay, but it appears to be incorrect for the model year. The tall valve covers hint at a 1970s version of the RB mill. It also includes a few other day-two mods .
While much of the red interior is still around to tell its story, the exterior color is a mystery. I've seen traces of Plum Crazy purple on the firewall, but Dodge did not offer this hue at the time. The floor panels show metallic blue, which was a factory option. On the flipside, it's a rather strange choice for a red interior.
However, I also noticed a bit of red paint on the door jambs, and a red-on-red layout would make sense. Or perhaps the white that still covers some section of the trunk may have something to do with the original finish.
Anyway, while this Coronet may look too far gone, someone decided to give it a second chance. One of the rear fenders was already replaced, while the other one was cut off for similar treatment. Steve says that the Coronet will be restored, which is terrific news for such a rare Mopar. But it may take a while until we see it back on the road.
